archetype.name: Retooling Year (bat-first, glove-poor)
archetype.definition: A club that climbed seven wins off a 70-92 bottom by rebuilding its offense but never fixed the run prevention that kept it under .500 and eight games out of the division.

report.headline: A better lineup, a leaky glove, and an August that erased July

recap.finish: 77-85, third in the AL Central, eight games behind Cleveland; missed the postseason
recap.body:
This was a sub-.500 team built to hit, and it did hit. The Twins scored their way from 23rd in the league to 10th, posted a .720 OPS (11th), and gave Derek Shelton a lineup with real on-base and power threats. What they could not do was keep runs off the board: 4.92 allowed per game ranked 25th, the staff ERA of 4.56 sat 25th, and the fielders cost 24.2 runs, 26th of 30. The -0.36 Run Diff / G says roughly a 75-win team, so 77-85 was, if anything, slightly kind.

The season had almost no streaks. The longest win streak was four, the longest skid five. Instead it moved in slow drifts. A 1-3 March and three near-.500 months (13-15, 13-15, 14-13) left them treading water, even though May (outscored 147-121) and June (156-146) were worse than their records. July was the high point at 15-9, and the team stood 56-55 at month's end. That July was built on a 102-98 run margin, a record ahead of the play. August then collapsed to 10-17 while getting outscored by 19, and 11-13 in September finished a 21-30 slide that turned a .500 club into a 77-win one. A 6-4 last ten games was too late to matter.

The offense ran on a handful of above-average bats. Luke Keaschall (123 wRC+, .374 OBP, 20 SB, 3.0 WAR) was the table-setter, Byron Buxton (128 wRC+, 25 HR in 93 games) made the All-Star team, and Trevor Larnach (123) and Ryan Jeffers (128) hit well in partial roles. Kody Clemens added 27 homers. The hitters' C grade comes from the holes: Royce Lewis got 509 PA with an 85 wRC+ at first base, and Victor Caratini got more trips than Jeffers (382 to 369) while posting a 79. Buxton's 93 games mattered too. Some of the slugging also gets a lift from a 106 park.

The pitching story is more forgiving than the ERA. The rotation graded a B. Taj Bradley (3.73 ERA, 205 K) and All-Star Joe Ryan (3.79, 5% walks) were a sound top two. Connor Prielipp's 4.87 ERA came with a 3.73 FIP, and Andrew Morris's 4.40 ERA came with a 3.29 FIP. Gaps that size point at the defense behind them, and Keaschall's -12.5 Def Runs is about half the team's fielding deficit by himself. The back of the rotation was genuinely mediocre, though: Bailey Ober and Zebby Matthews combined for about 261 innings at a 4.47 and a 4.90. The C+ bullpen leaned on Jeff Hoffman (2.48 FIP, 34.9% K). Its closer, Yoendrys Gómez, walked 13.1% of batters on his way to 22 saves.

Against the recent past, this is a partial recovery. It sits well short of 2023's 87 wins and the third-best run prevention in the league. The offense is back near its 2023-24 level. The run prevention has now ranked 23rd and 25th in consecutive seasons, and the fielding got twice as bad as in 2025.

highlights.title: Offense rebuilt from the bottom
highlights.body: Runs per game jumped from 23rd in 2025 to 10th, back near the 2023-24 level. Keaschall's on-base work and the 120-plus wRC+ seasons from Buxton, Jeffers and Larnach drove it. The 106 park flatters the raw totals a little. The wRC+ figures are park-adjusted, though, and the core of the lineup is real.

highlights.title: A legitimate front two
highlights.body: Bradley and Ryan combined for about 323 innings with ERAs under 3.80, and their FIPs back those ERAs up. Bradley missed bats at 27.4% and Ryan barely walked anyone. Those two are the main reason the rotation graded a B despite a 25th-ranked staff ERA.

highlights.title: Hoffman anchored the bullpen
highlights.body: Hoffman struck out 34.9% of hitters with a 2.48 FIP and ranked 12th of 389 relievers. The 3.55 ERA understates him. He was the one reliever the numbers say was clearly good.

lowlights.title: Defense gave the runs back
lowlights.body: Fielders cost 24.2 runs, 26th in the league, double the 2025 deficit. Keaschall's -12.5 Def Runs accounts for half of it. The ERA-FIP gaps for Prielipp and Morris show where those runs landed. This is fixable but structural: the team's best on-base bat is also its worst glove.

lowlights.title: August sank a .500 team
lowlights.body: At 56-55 after July, the Twins went 10-17 in August, getting outscored by 19, and 21-30 the rest of the way. July's 15-9 had come on a +4 run margin, so the drop was partly a correction of a record running ahead of the play.

lowlights.title: Lineup holes got big playing time
lowlights.body: Lewis took 509 PA with an 85 wRC+ from first base. Caratini out-batted Jeffers in playing time despite a 79 wRC+ against Jeffers' 128. Those two spots dragged the hitters to a C grade around a strong core.

arc.note: Near .500 for four months with almost no streaks, peaked at 56-55 after a fortunate July, then went 21-30 over August and September.

recap.nextYear: The bats that carried this team are the ones to build around: Keaschall's on-base skill, Buxton's power (if he plays more than 93 games), and Jeffers and Larnach, who earned bigger shares of the plate appearances that went to Lewis and Caratini. The rotation's B grade rests on Bradley and Ryan. Prielipp's 3.73 FIP says he is better than his ERA, while Ober and Matthews are the soft spots. The bullpen needs more than Hoffman, and a closer walking 13.1% is a risk. The clearest lever is defense: -24.2 Fielding Runs, half from one second baseman, is the gap between a staff that pitches like its FIPs and one that ranks 25th in run prevention. The +1.6 W vs Run Diff means the record was slightly lucky, so true talent was nearer 75 wins. A real climb has to come from run prevention, not from banking on close games.

confidence.note: Full 162-game season; ERA-FIP gaps leave some room on how much was defense versus luck.
